newsitem.title: USA: House conferees to drop de minimis repeal for now.
newsitem.headline: House conferees to drop de minimis repeal for now.

text.p: U.S. House tax conferees have tentatively agreed to back off from their chamber's proposed repeal of the two-percent de minimis exclusion, a delighted municipal industry source said Thursday.

"There's a tentative agreement," the source said. "But it's still going to be on the table while they work with the Administration. The situation is still very fluid. We've crossed a hurdle, but we're not there yet."

The source said House conferees also agreed to adopt the Senate's proposal to repeal altogether the current $150 million cap on non-hospital borrowing by 501(c)(3) groups, in more good news for the muni market.
The House originally wanted a narrower plan that would raise the limit by $10 million a year for five years - for a total cap of $200 million.

And House conferees tentatively accepted the Senate's plan to increase from $5 million to $10 million the arbitrage rebate exception for small municipal issuers of bonds used to finance public school infrastructure costs, the source said.
Currently, the Internal Revenue Service does not permit businesses to deduct interest on debt that they use to finance the purchase of tax-exempt bonds.

But IRS said in 1972 -- in what has been dubbed the de minimis rule -- that it will not monitor whether a corporation has borrowed to purchase tax-exempt bonds as long as those holdings total less than two percent of net assets.

The Clinton Administration this winter called for repeal of the two percent de minimis rule, dubbing it corporate welfare. And the House voted to repeal the exception for corporate holdings of munis over $1 million.
The Senate tax bill, however, is silent on the issue.
House tax bill negotiators have been deluged with letters from state and local officials nationwide urging them not to repeal de minimis.

"We're pleased to see that congressional leaders are listening to their constituents, and that they are weighing the concerns of state and local governments as they put together the tax bill," the muni source said.
